forces: Orchestra, organ and piano four hands
performers: Philharmonic-Symphony Orchestra of New York; Charles Munch; Édouard Nies-Berger, organ
intro: Part II of the “Organ” Symphony opens with a C minor scherzo and a Presto with scales in both hands for the piano, after which the organ enters with a huge C major chord. In Munch’s 1947 reading, a long quiet passage over G leads to that chord.

sections.label: A · Scherzo, Allegro moderato, C minor
B · Presto in C major, with piano scales
Link · Soft build over pedal G
sections.mNote: A soft pedal G leads to the organ’s C major.

sections.label: C · Maestoso, organ chord and chorale
sections.mNote: The main theme returns as a chorale.

cues.title: Scherzo in C minor
cues.text: The second half opens with a scherzo, back in C minor.
cues.evidence: Hugh Macdonald’s programme note on the Symphony No. 3, Boston Symphony Orchestra. https://www.bso.org/works/saint-saens-symphony-no-3-organ-symphony The note places the scherzo at the start of the second movement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Presto in C major, piano scales
cues.text: The Presto is in C major. The piano plays a series of scales in both hands.
cues.evidence: Hugh Macdonald’s programme note on the Symphony No. 3, Boston Symphony Orchestra. https://www.bso.org/works/saint-saens-symphony-no-3-organ-symphony The note describes the Presto and the piano’s both-hand scales.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Liszt
cues.text: The composer had intended to dedicate the symphony to Liszt, who died that July. The published dedication reads “to the memory of Franz Liszt”. When the work was heard in Paris, Gounod is reported to have called it the French Beethoven.
cues.evidence: Hugh Macdonald’s programme note on the Symphony No. 3, Boston Symphony Orchestra, gives the intended dedication, the published “à la mémoire de Franz Liszt” and Gounod’s remark “Voilà le Beethoven français!” https://www.bso.org/works/saint-saens-symphony-no-3-organ-symphony The Société Camille Saint-Saëns chronology also dedicates the work to Liszt, who died without hearing it. https://camille-saint-saens.org/1882-1888/ Sources differ on whether Liszt heard any of the symphony, so the note claims only the dedication.

cues.title: Opening of the Maestoso finale
cues.text: The finale, marked Maestoso, opens with a C major chord on the organ. The main theme returns as a chorale.
cues.evidence: The Internet Archive item for Columbia Masterworks set MM-747, with the transferor’s side-by-side description. https://archive.org/details/mm-747-saint-saens-sym-3-i The transferor puts the finale at 6:55 in this file; the organ plays on sides 7 and 8. Hugh Macdonald’s programme note on the Symphony No. 3, Boston Symphony Orchestra. https://www.bso.org/works/saint-saens-symphony-no-3-organ-symphony

cues.title: Piano duet, upper register
cues.text: A second pianist joins the first, and the two play in the upper register. Saint-Saëns took this sonority from Berlioz’s Lélio, of which he made the piano reduction at nineteen.
cues.evidence: Hugh Macdonald’s programme note on the Symphony No. 3, Boston Symphony Orchestra. https://www.bso.org/works/saint-saens-symphony-no-3-organ-symphony The note describes the piano duet and its debt to Lélio.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Performers and label credits
cues.text: The organist, Nies-Berger, is credited on every label but plays only on sides 3, 4, 7 and 8. The pianists of the four-hand part are uncredited on the labels; Pristine’s reissue names Walter Hendl and Arthur Schuller.
cues.evidence: The Internet Archive item for Columbia Masterworks set MM-747, with the transferor’s side-by-side description of the sides and credits. https://archive.org/details/mm-747-saint-saens-sym-3-i Pristine Audio’s PASC448 page lists Walter Hendl and Arthur Schuller, piano, with Nies-Berger, organ. https://www.pristineclassical.com/products/pasc448

cues.title: Saint-Saëns on the symphony
cues.text: Saint-Saëns said that he had given this symphony all that he had to give, and that he would never do again what he had done there.
cues.evidence: Hugh Macdonald’s programme note on the Symphony No. 3, Boston Symphony Orchestra. https://www.bso.org/works/saint-saens-symphony-no-3-organ-symphony The note closes with the composer’s remark.

composer.epithet: Pianist from the age of ten and organist for twenty years, known for the Organ Symphony, a dance of skeletons featuring xylophone, and a zoo suite he forbade anyone to publish.
facts: Piano with Stamaty; organ with François Benoist and composition under Halévy at the Paris Conservatoire, from 1848
Organist of La Madeleine, 1857–77; piano professor at the École Niedermeyer, 1861–65; co-founder of the Société nationale de musique, 1871
Symphonies, ten concertos, four symphonic poems, operas, organ music, songs and chamber music; also plays, poems and articles
Spent most winters from 1873 in Algeria, Egypt or the Canary Islands, and kept no fixed address from 1889 to 1905

quote.text: I have given it all that I had to give. What I have done I shall never do again.
quote.source: Saint-Saëns on the Organ Symphony, as quoted in Hugh Macdonald’s Boston Symphony Orchestra note

composer.background:
Camille Saint-Saëns was born at 3 rue du Jardinet in Paris on 9 October 1835. His father, a clerk in the Ministry of the Interior, died of consumption on 30 December, when the boy was not yet three months old. He was a sickly child and was raised by two widows, his mother Clémence and her aunt Charlotte Masson, who taught him piano. At two and a half he pressed the keys one at a time and waited for each note to die away before playing the next. By his own account he already listened at that age to the kettle on the drawing-room fire, which he called a “microscopic oboe”, and to its sound swelling until the water boiled.

Children’s pieces gave the left hand nothing to do. “The bass doesn’t sing,” he told his teachers in disgust, and was given Haydn and Mozart. On 6 May 1846, aged ten, he played Beethoven’s Third Piano Concerto and a Mozart concerto in B♭ at the Salle Pleyel, and played the whole programme from memory. Someone asked his mother what he would play when he was twenty. “He will play his own,” she said.
